entries.definition: The gap between what the audience knows and what a character knows. It is a writer's method: the writer arranges for the audience to be told, or to work out, something a character on stage has not.
entries.example: Birling calls the Titanic unsinkable in a play set in spring 1912 and watched in 1945; the audience knows she sank within weeks. Mrs Birling demands that the father of the child be punished while the audience has already worked out that he is Eric.

entries.definition: Anything a playwright builds to do a job in the play: a character who carries the argument, an object that proves or conceals, a timing that protects a speech. Writing about a character as a device means saying what the writer does with them, not what they are like.
entries.example: The Inspector is a device: his one-at-a-time questioning proves the chain, and his exit before the doubt is raised keeps the final speech safe from suspicion. The photograph is a device: seen singly, it proves each link and later offers the family a loophole.

entries.definition: How a play is built across its whole length: the order of events, where the acts end, how time passes, what is delayed and what is repeated. In the exam, structure is a writer's method and earns AO2 marks when its effect is explained.
entries.example: An Inspector Calls runs in continuous time in one room, questions five people in the order they met the girl, ends each act on a cliffhanger, and finishes with a telephone call that starts the evening again.

entries.definition: The playwright's instructions on the page for how a line is delivered, how a character moves, what the set and lighting are like. They are part of the writer's method, because a play is written to be performed, and the June 2024 mark scheme lists them among the methods an essay can analyse.
entries.example: A direction that a character is distressed, or that the lighting changes when the Inspector arrives, is a choice by Priestley about how the audience should see the moment; naming it and saying what it does is AO2.

entries.definition: The circumstances a text was written in and about, and the ideas of its time, used to explain choices the writer made. AO3 rewards context that explains a method or a moment; a paragraph of history on its own earns almost nothing.
entries.example: Priestley set the play in 1912 so that an audience of 1945 would hear Birling's forecasts as dramatic irony; he gave the committee to Mrs Birling because in 1912 the charity of ladies stood where a welfare state would.

entries.definition: A medieval form of drama in which a representative figure, often called Everyman, is visited by figures such as Death or Conscience and made to account for his life. Modern plays borrow the shape when a visitor makes a household answer for what it has done.
entries.example: The Inspector calls on the Birlings and makes each account for one act; the girl with the commonest of names stands for everyone. Naming the form and what Priestley does with it is context and method at once.

entries.definition: A nineteenth-century form of tightly plotted drama: one setting, continuous or near-continuous time, secrets revealed in sequence, and a curtain line at the end of every act. Priestley keeps all of it, which is why the play feels like a machine closing on the family.
entries.example: Act 1 of An Inspector Calls ends on Gerald's reaction to the name Daisy Renton, Act 2 on the realisation about Eric, Act 3 on the telephone: three curtain lines in the well-made tradition.

entries.definition: An examination in which no copy of the text is allowed. Both AQA Literature papers are closed book: an extract is printed for the Shakespeare and novel questions and one poem for the poetry comparison, but the modern text essay has no extract at all, so every quotation comes from memory.
entries.example: For the An Inspector Calls essay a student carries in one exact line for each character and each theme, such as the Inspector's line that we are members of one body.

entries.definition: The part of an AQA mark scheme that lists what an answer to a particular question might include, under AO1, AO2 and AO3. It is not a checklist, and the scheme says any valid interpretation is rewarded, but its three columns are the shape of a strong plan.
entries.example: For the June 2024 question on Mrs Birling and social class, the AO2 bullets were her words and manner of speech, the contrast with Sheila and Eric, the dramatic revelation of her involvement, and the stage directions about her.

entries.definition: The way AQA marks an essay: the whole answer is placed in one of six levels by its overall quality, then given a mark within that level. Level 1 is simple and narrative in approach; Level 6 is convincing, critical, exploratory and conceptualised. Each level has a mark range and descriptor words.
entries.example: On the thirty-mark An Inspector Calls essay, Level 4 (16 to 20) is clear understanding with effective references; Level 6 (26 to 30) is a conceptualised argument with fine-grained analysis of methods and judicious references.

aliases: an idea about the whole text
entries.definition: The word the Level 6 descriptor uses for an essay led by an idea about the whole text, which every paragraph then serves, as opposed to an answer that works through points, or the plot, one by one.
entries.example: Priestley builds a play in which four themes are one argument: responsibility is the claim, class the reason it is refused, age the hope, and the girl's life the evidence. An essay opened with that sentence is conceptualised; one that takes each theme in turn is a list.

entries.definition: In An Inspector Calls, the sequence of five encounters that pushed the girl from one door to the next: Birling, Sheila, Gerald, Mrs Birling, Eric, in the order she met them, which is also the order the Inspector questions them. Each link is worse because of the one before it.
entries.example: Sheila's jealous complaint at Milwards would have been a small cruelty if the girl had still had her first job; it becomes the second door shut because Birling has already shut the first.

entries.definition: In An Inspector Calls, the split that appears at the end of the play between the older characters, who treat the doubt about the Inspector as the end of the matter, and the younger ones, who accept what they did whatever he was. Gerald, young but on the side of the parents, shows that the real line is drawn by who accepts responsibility.
entries.example: Sheila's line that her parents do not seem to have learnt anything is the theme in one sentence; Priestley, writing in 1945, gives the capacity to change to the generation that would rebuild the country.
